Oct 9 : Norse Atlantic Airways will lease two Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners to Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), it said on Friday, in the latest move by the struggling Norwegian airline to shore up its finances. The agreement helps Norse retain a key ACMI (aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance) contract after India's largest airline IndiGo in July said it would end its wet-lease arrangement with the Norwegian group. Norse, faced with soaring jet fuel costs, has been reducing its exposure to low-cost transatlantic services and increasing its focus on ACMI, under which it leases aircraft and crews to other airlines for a fee. • Flight operations for flag carrier PIA are scheduled to begin in November 2026

FAST

SEOUL/TOKYO: South Korean and Japanese companies are racing to strengthen cyber defences after a wave of attacks that cybersecurity experts say are highlighting how AI may be lowering the bar for criminals with limited technical skills. Nine South Korean banks and two mega-churches are probing cyberattacks that may have involved AI tools, while Japanese companies including Daiwa Securities, SoftBank and the Lawson convenience store chain have been hit by a recent surge in cyber incidents. Authorities are still investigating whether and how AI was used in many of the breaches. But cybersecurity specialists say the technology is helping attackers automate tasks from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect. "AI doesn't get tired ... My view is that Japan is essentially being subjected to carpet bombing," said Nobuo Miwa, president of Tokyo-based cybersecurity firm S&J Corp.

Japan recorded more cybersecurity incidents in the first nine months of the year than in all of last year, according to data from TrendAI. Incidents rose to 86 in September, up about 18 per cent from August and 37 per cent from July. The rise suggests attackers have crossed a threshold in "effort, motivation and technical capability", while AI has largely erased language and other barriers that once hindered foreign hackers, Miwa said. US cybersecurity company CrowdStrike said a suspected 26-year-old China-based attacker behind the South Korean bank incidents would probably not have been able to carry out the campaign without AI assistance.  The individual, whom CrowdStrike assessed was pursuing financial gain, used a Chinese-developed AI agent and Anthropic's Claude Code, according to the company. "While (the hacker's) capabilities were not terribly sophisticated they were effective," said Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary operations.

Related:

CrowdStrike says China-based suspect used AI tools in South Korean bank hacks

South Korea's Lee says AI appears to have been used in bank hacks

HARD-TO-DETECT ATTACKS AI-powered tools are also making it harder for defenders to spot suspicious behaviour, said Choi Kyoungjin, director of the Center for AI, Data and Policy at Gachon University near Seoul. "With general-purpose AI models, even ordinary users with malicious intent can ask the system to look for vulnerabilities and it will do much of that work for them," he said.  South Korea reported 1,236 cyber incidents in the first half of the year, up 20 per cent from a year earlier. While server hacking cases fell, reports of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks and ransomware rose 56.7 per cent and 76.8 per cent respectively, according to government data. The South Korean bank incidents underscored the need for stronger security controls and more rigorous testing as AI evolves, Meyers said. "The genie is out of the bottle, so to speak." Although the breaches have not yet resulted in material financial losses, risks could increase if stolen data is used in phishing or similar text-message "smishing" campaigns, Karen Wu, senior analyst at Fitch, wrote in a note.  "We expect the incidents to result in regulatory penalties, customer compensation costs, and a sector-wide increase in cybersecurity spending," Wu said.

Related:

Singapore studying stronger safeguards for high-risk AI uses as systems grow more autonomous: Josephine Teo

Australia says OpenAI agent hacked into government website

DEFENCES NEED THEIR OWN BREAKTHROUGH Warnings about AI's growing role in cybercrime are increasingly coming from the technology's developers. Alphabet's Google and Anthropic have both warned that AI-assisted attacks are becoming more common globally. “At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited,” John Hultquist, the chief analyst at Google’s Threat Intelligence Group, said last month.  Regulators in Japan and South Korea have begun responding. South Korea's Financial Services Commission has directed financial industry associations, regulators and affected executives to complete a 12-point cybersecurity self-assessment.  In Japan, digital transformation minister Toshiharu Furukawa convened a meeting of ministries and agencies on Thursday following the recent attacks. The National Cybersecurity Office plans to issue warnings to businesses.  S&J's Miwa said he expected elevated levels of cyberattacks to persist. "The attackers have experienced a breakthrough that has rendered many of the old assumptions obsolete," he said. "Our defences need their own breakthrough as well."

Source: Reuters/aj

FAST

SYDNEY, Oct 9 : The collapse of Nvidia-backed data centre operator Firmus' $5 billion IPO is a blow to Australia's capital markets which are already facing a shrinking pool of listed entities, investors said. Australia's benchmark share index is heavily skewed to the Big Four banks and huge mining companies, so some money managers had hoped a big tech listing would make the market more attractive by offering more choice to investors. Firmus pulled its listing plans on Friday, citing market volatility and conditions, and said it would pursue a private fundraising round instead. At $5 billion, the closely-watched IPO would have ranked as the fourth-largest public offering globally so far this year, behind SpaceX, CXMT Corp and Cerebras Systems, according to Dealogic data.

It would also be the second-largest IPO for the Australian Securities Exchange on record, behind only Telstra Corp's $10 billion flotation in 1997. The withdrawal is a setback for the ASX, which has been grappling with a declining number of listed companies after several major privatisations in recent years and a weak pipeline of new listings, investors said. "It's really bad," said Oscar Oberg, lead portfolio manager at Wilson Asset Management, referencing the capital market implications of the deal's collapse. WAM has been a Firmus investor since last year. "We owned shares early, I'm not going to hide behind that. But I just think it would have been good for the market to have something new." "The lack of IPOs has been very frustrating for a long, long time for us … that to me is the most disappointing part." There were just $1.37 billion worth of new share sales in Australia in the first nine months of 2026, according to LSEG data, the most since 2021, but well below global rival exchanges. Hong Kong, for example, has seen 118 companies, mainly those from the technology sector, raising around $50 billion via IPOs in that period, according to the data from the Hong Kong stock exchange. The ASX has also steadily lost listed companies, particularly in the infrastructure sector, to takeovers by private enterprises, said Jamie Hannah, deputy head of Investments and Capital Markets at VanEck Australia. In September 2026, there were 1,891 companies listed on the ASX, down from 2,066 in 2016, according to the market operator. "It's a blow to the market, not getting off one of these big listings," Hannah said. "We do want to see bigger transactions take place on the market. And I think most Australians who invest would like to see more opportunities as well." Hannah said that while Firmus' IPO failure was largely to do with the nature of the company, it was also a blow for the market's diversity, which is heavily concentrated between the so-called Big Four banks and major miners like BHP and Rio Tinto. In what would further bolster miners' concentration, London-listed miner Glencore expects to begin trading on the ASX on October 14, and its CEO said on Friday the company had seen "very strong" interest from potential investors. "We're very overweight in the materials resource sector and obviously in financials. They're the backbone of the Australian market and it also creates cyclical performance based on individual overweights in each of those sectors," Hannah said.

Source: Reuters

Oct 9 : OpenAI fired three of its researchers last week after an investigation found they violated policies on handling sensitive information, the AI major said in a post on X on Friday. OpenAI's statement comes after the dismissed researchers Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni published a letter outlining the circumstances of their termination, expressing concern over how it was handled.  "Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment," OpenAI said.  Wang, Korbak, and Balesni said in their letter that they were not the source of a news article published on The Information last month about security concerns around OpenAI's latest AI model.

FAST

NEW YORK: US immigration agents shot and wounded a man on Thursday (Oct 8) in his car with a child present in the Marble Hill neighbourhood of New York City, according to the mayor, city police and eyewitnesses. Federal immigration agents have shot at least 21 people since Republican President Donald Trump returned to office, 7 fatally , sparking protests across the US. Critics contend that Trump's push to ramp up deportations has led to an increasing number of violent confrontations, and accuse the administration of resisting accountability for the agents involved. Trump has said many migrants must be deported, blaming them, often in sweeping terms, for financial fraud and violent crimes. "Early reports indicate agents surrounded (the man) and a 5-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds," New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement.

"I have been on the phone with President Trump and (Homeland Security) Secretary Mullin, negotiating the release of the man Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful," Mamdani said in a press conference late in the evening. He said he demanded from the Trump administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City. "These actions are making the city less safe," Mamdani said. "This city wants ICE out. We want ICE out of our city, ICE out of our schools, ICE out of our hospitals, ICE out of our streets, ICE away from our kids."

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference at the scene of a shooting reportedly involving US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in the Bronx borough of New York City on Oct 8, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Eduardo Munoz)

The mayor said the child in the car is physically unharmed. New York Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said NYPD has located the child with a family member after a wellness check. The Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, said in a statement ICE officers were conducting a "targeted enforcement operation" in the Bronx, New York, to arrest a man from the Dominican Republic with a prior criminal conviction. The man identified as 28-year-old, had been arrested twice in New York City in 2023 and 2025, according to NYPD Commissioner Tisch. "During the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon and the criminal illegal alien was injured," DHS said, adding that ICE officers rendered immediate aid. "The individual is alive and at a local hospital." The shooting occurred at around 4pm ET (2000 GMT), DHS said. Working at a restaurant near the shooting, Pedro Almarez said he heard shots fired and went outside to see several officers wearing ICE attire at the scene. "There were a lot of ICE officers, three or four cars," Almarez told Reuters by phone. He said NYPD officers arrived about 10 minutes later. He said the man was only removed from his car after an ambulance arrived. At the shooting scene, where police strung yellow crime-scene tape to cordon off a city block, a woman standing on a balcony overlooking the area told officers they were "taking our children", according to a Reuters witness.

Oct 9 : SoftBank Group CEO Masayoshi Son is seeking to raise up to $100 billion from Gulf investors to fund a new wave of AI investments, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. Son has held discussions in recent weeks with senior figures, including in the United Arab Emirates, about the potential fundraising, the report said. Reuters couldn't immediately verify the report. SoftBank did not respond to a request for comment. The move comes as Son ramps up AI bets, with the company announcing last week that it completed its $30 billion investment in OpenAI as part of its commitment to the ChatGPT maker's last fundraising round. SoftBank also raised $11.1 billion last month in the largest high-yield corporate bond sale globally to fund its mammoth bet on OpenAI. The Japanese investment conglomerate would use the proceeds to establish a fund that would acquire companies and improve their operations using AI and other advanced technologies, according to the report.

FAST

Facebook and Instagram-owner Meta has banned advertisements by ByteDance, the Chinese parent of TikTok, on its platforms in the United States and a handful of other countries, a company spokesperson said on Thursday (Oct 8). The move marks an escalation in the long-running rivalry between Meta and ByteDance, whose video-sharing app TikTok has emerged as one of Meta's most formidable competitors for user engagement, creators and advertising dollars. Meta's ban takes effect immediately in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, and extends to third-party advertisers running campaigns that link to TikTok and other ByteDance properties in those countries, Meta said. "We don't have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps," Meta said. "Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience."

TikTok and ByteDance did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment on Meta's move. TikTok's website shows that it does not support links that open or log users into other social media apps. However, users can still add links to their profiles that direct people to those platforms' websites. Meta has been urging TikTok and YouTube to follow steps it agreed to take on teen safety in August following a settlement of up to US$18 billion with US states over social media harms to children. Meta in August agreed to impose daily usage limits and restrict nighttime usage by children who use Facebook and Instagram, and enhance measures to prevent children from accessing age-restricted content. TikTok has not publicly commented on Meta's campaign, but it reached a settlement with Alabama in September that requires the social media platform to impose new usage limits and enhance age-verification measures for users in the state, resolving claims that it endangered children and misled consumers about its safety. TikTok operates in the US as a majority American-owned joint venture after a deal aimed at safeguarding US user data and averting a US ban on an app used by more than 200 million users in the country. Bloomberg News first reported Meta's ban earlier on Thursday.

Oct 9 : New Zealand batter Mark Chapman and fast-bowler Zak Foulkes have been ruled out of the Twenty20 series against India due to injuries, the country's cricket board (NZC) said on Friday. • New Zealand host India in five T20s, five one-day internationals (ODIs) and two tests, with the opening T20 in Christchurch on October 22. • Chapman suffered a left hamstring tear during the European T20 League last month but is expected to be available for the ODI series against India. • Foulkes injured his right hip flexor during a recent Canterbury men's training session, with no timeline yet set for his return.

NEW YORK: Protesters calling for tougher action against sexual violence rallied on Thursday (Oct 8) outside the New York City courthouse where a Cornell University student stirred a national uproar by suing several campus fraternity members she accused of gang rape. The demonstration, drawing a crowd of hundreds to the New York State Supreme Court building in Manhattan, was one of dozens of protests organised on campuses and in communities across the country under the social media banner "#StopSexualViolence: From the Frat House to the White House." Several hundred people, mostly women, displayed banners reading “I am Jane Doe. Be afraid of me”, “Death to rape culture” and “This is personal” outside the New York Supreme Court in downtown Manhattan, where the Cornell student identified in court documents as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against her alleged rapists. “It's entirely frustrating that we are here in 2026 and still dealing with this,” said one of the protesters, Brianna Williams, 40, who works for a nonprofit. “It's just an infuriating moment.”

In a lawsuit filed last month, a Cornell student identified by the pseudonym Jane Doe said she had been plied with drugs and alcohol, then sexually assaulted by members of the campus chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity while she was incapacitated in October 2024. Doe, who was 20 at the time, named seven Chi Phi members as defendants in the suit, along with the fraternity, a local bar, her own sorority, and the Ivy League university, which she accused of failing to adequately investigate and punish students who were involved. The lawsuit specifically criticised the university for having offered some of the alleged perpetrators a chance to mitigate their penalties by writing essays. Doe had reported the alleged assault to police several weeks after the fact, leading to an internal university investigation and a law enforcement probe, but the local prosecutor declined to bring criminal charges in the case. Since the woman's civil suit was filed, prosecutors reopened a criminal investigation, and New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed the state's attorney general as special prosecutor in the case. Cornell University hired Sally Yates, a top former US Justice Department lawyer, to lead an independent review of how the school handled the allegations. NATIONAL OUTCRY Cornell, which has defended its response to the original report, shut down the Chi Phi chapter and imposed a range of discipline on the fraternity members found to be involved, including expulsions of some. The men named in the suit have all denied any wrongdoing, some saying the sexual activity was consensual and others disputing their participation. The suit ignited a renewed national outcry against sexual violence and harassment, especially on college campuses, with women taking to the streets in "I Am Jane Doe" protests of solidarity. "I Am Jane Doe" was also a rallying cry for Thursday's scheduled demonstrations in cities including Washington, Philadelphia, Boston, Denver, Salt Lake City, Los Angeles and San Francisco. Some activists have pointed to comments from President Donald Trump about his behaviour toward women and a jury verdict finding him liable for sexual abuse of writer E Jean Carroll as contributing to a "culture of rape" in the US. Thousands of students, faculty and community activists marched on Monday through the Cornell campus in Ithaca, New York, demanding that the school administration take firmer action against sexual violence on campus. The identity of Jane Doe has become part of the conversation. Women on social media have been posting #IamJaneDoe in solidarity with the accuser and to counter those who have sought to publicly name her.
